Lessons.Title: What are Perfect Squares?
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: recognize algebraic perfect-square trinomials, derive identities (x±n)²=x²±2nx+n² and determine why the middle coefficient must be twice the product. Original independent Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 11 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/11/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/11/index.html (CC BY 4.0). Source establishes structure for later completing the square.
Original examples x²+12x+36=(x+6)² and x²−10x+25=(x−5)². Expand (x+6)(x+6)=x²+6x+6x+36; the middle term12x comes from TWO cross terms. A scaled expression (2x+3)² expands to4x²+12x+9, not4x²+6x+9.

The pattern x²+bx+c is a perfect square when c=(b/2)² for monic leading coefficient1 and matching sign. Thus x²+8x+16 is a perfect square, but x²+8x+12 is not one of this exact monic pattern with a single repeated linear factor.

Student task: build two square diagrams, classify trinomials as perfect/nonperfect, explain the missing cross term in a wrong expansion and derive a general identity. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for diagram/structure, exact expansions, valid criteria and error analysis.
